questions.question: What are Spring bean scopes?
questions.title: Spring Bean Scopes Overview
questions.direct_answer: A Spring scope controls how a bean instance is obtained and how long the container manages it. singleton is one instance per bean definition per ApplicationContext and is the default. prototype creates a new instance each time the container is asked for that bean. In a web-aware context, request, session, application, and websocket scopes follow their respective web lifetimes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know all five bean scopes and can explain when each is appropriate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only mentioning singleton and prototype, forgetting the three web scopes (request, session, application)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the prototype-in-singleton problem and how Spring uses scoped proxies to inject web scopes into singletons

sections.title: Spring Bean Scopes
sections.content:
Scope does not make code thread-safe. A singleton with mutable request data can race, while a prototype passed between threads can also race. Prefer immutable or stateless services and use a narrower scope only when the state truly follows that lifetime.

Prototype destruction is the caller's responsibility after Spring hands out the object. Custom scopes can define other lifecycles, so descriptions such as 'new every request' must name whether request means a bean lookup or an HTTP request.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: singleton means shared in one container, not one object per JVM or class.
prototype means a new result per container lookup, not automatically per HTTP request.
Spring creates prototype instances but normally does not run their destruction callbacks.
@RequestScope and @SessionScope use scoped proxies by default for safe injection into longer-lived beans.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For example, OrderService is normally a stateless singleton. A request-scoped RequestContext can hold one request's correlation data and be injected through its scoped proxy. A prototype ReportBuilder injected directly into a singleton is resolved once at singleton construction; use ObjectProvider.getObject() when a new builder is required for each operation.

sections.title: Bean Scopes at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|singleton|~Default, one per context|Shared instance|Should be stateless|Created eagerly
blue|prototype|~New each request|getBean returns a new object|Spring won't destroy it|Stateful helpers
emerald|request / session|~Web scopes|One per HTTP request|One per user session|Need a web context
violet|Rule of Thumb|~Match state to scope|Stateless to singleton|Stateful to prototype|Never store state in a singleton

sections.title: Singleton vs Prototype at a Glance
sections.content:
| Aspect | Singleton | Prototype |
|---|---|---|
| Instances | One per ApplicationContext | A new one every request |
| Default? | Yes | No, opt in with @Scope("prototype") |
| Best for | Stateless services | Stateful, short-lived beans |
| Destruction callback | @PreDestroy runs on context close | @PreDestroy never runs |
| Thread safety | Must be kept stateless | Each use is isolated |

sections.title: Mutable state in a singleton - data bug
Keep the singleton stateless
Defining Bean Scopes in Spring
When to Use Each Scope
sections.content:
Use **singleton** (the default) for stateless service classes like controllers, services, and repositories that hold no user-specific data. This is about 95% of your beans.

Use **prototype** when a bean has mutable state that shouldn't be shared — for example, a PDF generator that builds a report step by step, or a command object that accumulates user input.

Use **request** scope for beans that hold data valid only for one HTTP request, like a cart being checked out or search filters.

Use **session** scope for user-specific data that persists across multiple requests, like shopping cart contents, user preferences, or authentication state.

Use **application** scope for global shared state across all users, like app-wide configuration or metrics — rare in practice.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting web scopes exist**: Freshers often think Spring only has singleton and prototype, missing that request, session, and application scopes exist in web apps.
- **Using singleton for stateful beans**: Storing user-specific data (like current cart items) in a singleton bean causes one user to see another user's data because the instance is shared across all threads.
- **Not using a scoped proxy for web scopes**: Injecting a request or session scoped bean into a singleton without proxyMode=TARGET_CLASS fails because Spring can't put a short-lived bean into a long-lived one — you get a BeanCreationException at startup.

speakable_v2.hook: Scope answers one simple question. How many copies of a bean exist, and how long do they live?

beats.text: Bean scope tells Spring how many instances of a bean to make and how long they stick around. You set it with @Scope, and singleton is the default. And singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM.

Different beans need different lifetimes. A stateless service is fine to share, so one copy works. A stateful helper that builds up data can't be shared safely. Scope is how you match a bean's lifetime to its job.

items: Singleton: one shared instance per ApplicationContext. It's the default and works for stateless beans.
Prototype: a fresh instance every time you ask for the bean. It's for stateful beans.
Request: one instance per HTTP request. It dies when the request ends.
Session: one instance per user session. It lives until the session expires.
Application: one instance per ServletContext, shared across the whole web app.

beats.text: In a Spring Boot app, OrderService is a @Service, so it's singleton by default. Spring builds it once and injects the same one everywhere. A ReportBuilder that collects data gets @Scope prototype, so each report starts fresh. Here's the non-obvious part. Inject a prototype straight into a singleton and you only get one copy, which defeats the point.

items: Don't store per-user data in a singleton field. Concurrent requests will clobber each other.
Web scopes need proxyMode TARGET_CLASS when you inject them into a singleton.

speakable_v2.cap: Match the scope to the bean's lifetime. Stateless goes singleton, stateful goes prototype, and HTTP data goes to the web scopes.

questions.question: What is the singleton bean scope in Spring?
questions.title: Spring Singleton Bean Scope
questions.direct_answer: Singleton is Spring's default scope: one object is created and cached for one bean definition in one BeanFactory/ApplicationContext, then the same object is returned to callers. It is not one object per JVM. Stateless services are a simple safe use, but a singleton may hold shared state when that state and its collaborators are designed for concurrency and lifecycle requirements.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the most commonly used scope and its boundaries
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying singleton means one instance per JVM — it's actually one per ApplicationContext, so multiple contexts can have separate singleton instances
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why singleton beans must be stateless to be thread-safe in a multi-threaded web application

sections.title: Spring's Singleton Scope
sections.content:
Spring singleton identity is scoped to one bean definition. Two @Bean methods returning the same class normally create two distinct singleton beans. Aliases of one definition refer to the same object. A parent and child context can also contain separate beans of the same type/name subject to visibility rules.

Singletons are often created during context refresh unless lazy, but creation timing is separate from scope. Scope answers how resolutions map to instances, not exactly when initialization occurs.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Scope is per container and bean definition, not a Java static singleton.
The instance can be injected into many consumers and called by many request threads.
Mutable request-specific fields are unsafe without isolation/synchronization.
The container normally manages singleton initialization and destruction callbacks.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: OrderService is normally a singleton whose request data lives in method-local variables. A singleton metrics registry or cache deliberately holds mutable shared state and can be correct because its implementation is thread-safe. The rule is not 'no mutable fields'; it is 'do not store unsafely shared per-request state or mutate state without a concurrency design'. Two application contexts can each create their own instance.

emerald|Must Be Stateless|~Shared means thread-shared|No mutable instance fields|Use locals and params|Else race conditions
rose|Watch Out|~State bugs|Mutable field shared|Prototype-in-singleton trap|Use ObjectProvider

sections.title: Mutable field in a singleton - thread bug
Stateless singleton - thread-safe
Singleton Bean in Action
When to Use Singleton Scope
sections.content:
Use singleton scope for **stateless service classes** — beans that perform operations without storing mutable state in instance variables. Examples: @Service classes that orchestrate business logic, @Repository classes that talk to databases, @RestController classes that handle HTTP requests, and @Component utilities like validators or formatters. These beans typically have dependencies injected via the constructor and use only local variables within methods. Local variables are allocated per method call on the call stack, so they're naturally thread-safe. Singleton is the right choice for about 95% of your beans because it's memory-efficient and Spring manages the lifecycle automatically.

Avoid singleton when you need to store request-specific or user-specific data — that's when you need prototype, request, or session scope instead.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking singleton means one per JVM**: Freshers often say singleton creates one instance per JVM, but it's one per ApplicationContext. With a parent-child context hierarchy or multiple Spring apps in one JVM (like integration tests), you'll have multiple singleton instances.
- **Storing mutable state in instance variables**: Adding a field like private String currentUser to a singleton service causes thread-safety bugs. Thread A sets it to Alice, then Thread B sets it to Bob before Thread A's request finishes — now Thread A sees Bob's data.
- **Expecting singleton state to survive restarts**: Singleton instances are created when the ApplicationContext starts and destroyed on shutdown. They're not persisted, so state is lost between application restarts.

questions.question: What is the default scope for Spring beans and why?
questions.title: Why Singleton Is the Default Spring Bean Scope
questions.direct_answer: Singleton is a practical default because most infrastructure, repository, and service beans represent reusable collaborators rather than per-call state. The container creates one instance for each bean definition and shares it at injection points. That reduces construction and keeps one configured collaboration graph, but singleton scope alone does not make a bean stateless or thread-safe.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the architectural reasoning behind Spring's design decisions, not just the factual default value
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only stating that singleton is the default without explaining why it makes sense for typical enterprise architectures
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect statelessness to thread safety in servlet containers where many concurrent requests share the same bean instances

sections.title: Why Singleton Is Spring's Default Scope
sections.content: Spring's singleton is different from the classic global Singleton pattern: it is scoped to a container and bean definition, and tests or child contexts can have separate instances. Eager creation is common but @Lazy and other conditions can delay it. Thread safety follows the bean's implementation and its collaborators, not its scope label.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: The unit is one bean definition in one ApplicationContext.
Two bean definitions of the same class can still create two singleton instances.
Keep request-specific state in parameters/local values, not singleton fields.
Choose another scope for a real lifecycle need, not as a substitute for synchronization or design.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For example, one OrderRepository bean can be shared by OrderService and InvoiceService because its methods use call-local data and a thread-safe framework-managed EntityManager proxy. If OrderService stores currentCustomerId in a field, concurrent requests can overwrite it even though the bean is a valid Spring singleton.

sections.title: Request data in a singleton field - race bug
Pass per-request data as parameters
Singleton Bean Shared Across Multiple Consumers
When Singleton Scope is Appropriate
sections.content:
Use singleton scope (the default) for any **stateless bean**: services, repositories, controllers, validators, mappers, utilities. A bean is stateless if it doesn't store per-request or per-user data in instance fields. For example, a PaymentService that calls external APIs is stateless even though it has a WebClient field — that field is the same for all requests, not request-specific data. Configuration beans like DataSource or RestTemplate are perfect singletons: you want one shared connection pool, not hundreds. **ThreadLocal** patterns also work with singleton — each thread gets its own copy even though the bean instance is shared.

Avoid singleton only when you need **per-request state** (use request scope), **per-session state** (use session scope), or **per-operation mutable state** (use prototype).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Storing request data in singleton fields**: Freshers add instance fields like private String currentUserId to a singleton service and update them during request processing. Concurrent requests overwrite each other's data. Pass request-specific data as method parameters.
- **Thinking singleton means single-threaded**: Singleton doesn't mean only one thread uses the bean at a time. Hundreds of threads can call methods on the same instance concurrently, so any mutable shared state causes race conditions. Singleton plus stateless equals thread-safe.
- **Using prototype without reason**: Some freshers mark beans prototype thinking it's safer, but prototype creates a new instance per injection (not per method call), increases memory use, and is usually wrong unless the bean holds mutable per-use state.

questions.question: What is the prototype bean scope and when do you use it?
questions.title: Spring Prototype Bean Scope
questions.direct_answer: Prototype scope tells Spring to create a new bean instance each time that bean is requested from the container. It does not mean a new object appears on every method call, and a prototype injected once into a singleton is still that same injected instance. Spring performs initialization callbacks but does not manage complete destruction of prototype instances.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand when singleton scope is inappropriate and prototype is necessary
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that Spring doesn't manage the destruction lifecycle of prototype beans — no @PreDestroy callback runs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the prototype-in-singleton trap and all three fixes: ObjectProvider, @Lookup method injection, and ApplicationContext.getBean()

sections.title: What Prototype Scope Really Means
Quick revision
content: New instance per container resolution, such as getBean() or ObjectProvider.getObject().
One injection into a singleton resolves once unless a provider, lookup method, or scoped proxy is used.
Use prototype only when container-created per-use state is truly needed.
The caller owns cleanup after Spring hands over a prototype instance.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Prototype scope changes how BeanFactory resolves a bean. Calling getBean twice returns two instances. But when Spring constructs a singleton and injects one prototype into its constructor, that dependency is resolved only during singleton creation, so the singleton keeps it. To request a fresh instance per operation, inject ObjectProvider<Command> and call getObject(), use a lookup method, or choose an appropriate scoped proxy. Spring initializes a prototype and then releases lifecycle ownership, so @PreDestroy is not called automatically when the client finishes with it.

sections.title: Prototype Scope at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|What It Is|~New bean each time|Per getBean or injection|Never cached|Good for stateful objects
blue|Lifecycle Gap|~Spring steps back|Creates and wires it|No destroy callback|You manage cleanup
emerald|When to Use|~Stateful, short-lived|Per-request builders|Command objects|Non-thread-safe helpers
rose|The Classic Trap|~Inside a singleton|Injected once equals one instance|Use @Lookup or ObjectProvider|Or a scoped proxy

sections.title: Prototype injected directly - acts like a singleton
ObjectProvider gives a fresh prototype
Defining a Prototype Bean
When to Use Prototype Scope
sections.content:
Use prototype scope when you need **stateful beans** where each usage requires isolated mutable state. Examples: a report generator that accumulates data before rendering, a shopping cart being built up during checkout, a multi-step wizard that collects user input across pages, or a command object that validates and processes form data. Prototype is also useful for **beans with different configurations per usage** — imagine a file processor that needs different output formats (PDF, CSV, JSON) configured per request.

The key signal you need prototype: if reusing the bean instance would let one operation see data from a previous operation, or if two concurrent operations would corrupt each other's state.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Injecting prototype into singleton via constructor**: The most common mistake. Spring creates one prototype instance at startup and reuses it forever — you lose prototype behavior. Use ObjectProvider, @Lookup method injection, or getBean() to get a fresh instance each time.
- **Expecting Spring to call @PreDestroy**: Spring doesn't track prototype beans after creation, so @PreDestroy methods never run. If your prototype holds resources like file handles or connections, close them manually.
- **Using prototype when you need request or session scope**: Freshers sometimes use prototype for web-scoped data like user sessions. That's wrong — you'll get a new instance on every injection, not one per request or session.

questions.question: What are request and session scopes in Spring?
questions.title: Request and Session Scopes in Spring
questions.direct_answer: Request scope creates one bean instance for one HTTP request; session scope creates one per HTTP session. Injecting either directly into a longer-lived singleton needs deferred lookup, commonly a scoped proxy or ObjectProvider, because the real request or session instance does not exist when the singleton is created. The proxy mode is a common solution, not an unconditional requirement for every use.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand web-specific scopes and how they differ from singleton and prototype
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that proxyMode is required when injecting request or session scoped beans into singletons, causing startup errors
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a realistic session example like a shopping cart and explain how the scoped proxy delegates to the current request or session instance

sections.title: Request and Session Bean Lifetimes
sections.content:
A scoped proxy is a stable object injected into the singleton. Each method call on it finds the target for the current request or session. That is why one singleton service can safely refer to different request-scoped targets for simultaneous requests.

A proxy is not required when code asks the WebApplicationContext for the scoped bean during an active request, but direct lookup couples the code to the container. Provider lookup is another explicit option. Calling a request-scoped proxy outside an active request, such as from a background thread, fails because no request scope is bound there. Scope choice therefore includes both lifetime and where the bean may be used.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Request scope: one target instance per HTTP request.
Session scope: one target instance per HTTP session.
A scoped bean can be looked up directly inside an active request without a proxy.
A singleton dependency needs a scoped proxy or provider to resolve the current target later.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Web scopes tie bean storage to web context state. A request-scoped RequestContext can hold request-specific data and is destroyed when that request completes. A session-scoped Cart can survive across requests in one HTTP session. Problems arise when a singleton is created at startup and asks for a bean whose real instance exists only during a request. @RequestScope and @SessionScope use proxy defaults that make this common injection work, or the singleton can inject ObjectProvider. Avoid storing large or sensitive mutable state in sessions without a clear lifetime and concurrency policy.

sections.title: Request vs Session Scope
sections.content:
amber|request scope|~One per HTTP request|New for each request|Dies when request ends|Holds per-call data
blue|session scope|~One per user session|Spans many requests|Dies on session end|Holds per-user data
emerald|Requirement|~Web context only|Needs a web app|Fails in a plain context|Use a scoped proxy to inject
violet|Inject Into Singleton|~proxyMode needed|TARGET_CLASS proxy|Resolves the real bean per request|Else stale data

sections.title: Request vs Session Scope
sections.content:
| Aspect | Request Scope | Session Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifecycle | Created per HTTP request, destroyed when response sent | Created per user session, destroyed on timeout or logout |
| Typical use case | Search filters, form data, request-specific context | Shopping cart, user preferences, authentication state |
| Annotation | @RequestScope or @Scope(WebApplicationContext.SCOPE_REQUEST) | @SessionScope or @Scope(WebApplicationContext.SCOPE_SESSION) |
| Shared across requests | No, each request gets its own instance | Yes, the same instance across all requests in one session |
| Memory footprint | Low, destroyed quickly after each request | Higher, lives until the session expires (often 30 minutes idle) |

sections.title: Request bean injected directly - stale data
Scoped proxy resolves per request
When to Use Request and Session Scopes
sections.content:
Use **request scope** for data valid only for the duration of one HTTP request. Examples: user search filters, a temporary cart being checked out, request-specific audit context (user ID, correlation ID, IP address), or form submission data validated and processed in one request. Request scope keeps this data isolated so concurrent requests don't interfere.

Use **session scope** for user-specific data that persists across multiple requests. Examples: shopping cart contents built up over several pages, user preferences like language or theme, wizard state for multi-step forms, or authentication principal information. Session scope is cheaper than hitting a database or cache for every request, but watch memory — sessions can live 30 minutes after the last request.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting proxyMode when injecting into singletons**: The most common error. Without proxyMode=TARGET_CLASS, Spring throws a BeanCreationException at startup because it can't inject a shorter-lived bean into a longer-lived one. The proxy delays resolution until runtime.
- **Using session scope for data that belongs in the database**: Freshers store things like order history in session scope. Sessions expire, servers restart, and in a load-balanced setup session data might not replicate. Persistent data belongs in the database.
- **Not invalidating sessions on logout**: Session scoped beans live until you call HttpSession.invalidate(). If you don't, the old session can be hijacked or waste memory.

followup_questions: Why is proxyMode required for web-scoped beans in singletons?
Why wouldn't you use session scope in a stateless REST API?

beats.text: Request scope gives one bean per HTTP request. Session scope gives one per user session. Both differ from singleton, and singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM.

Pick request scope for data that lives inside one request and flows through your layers. Pick session scope for user state that must survive several requests, like a multi-step checkout. Skip session scope in stateless JWT APIs, since there's no server session to hold.

questions.question: What is the problem with injecting a prototype bean into a singleton in Spring?
questions.title: Prototype Bean in Singleton Problem
questions.direct_answer: When a **prototype** bean is injected into a **singleton** via constructor or field, Spring resolves it **only once** — at singleton creation — so the singleton reuses that single instance forever, silently defeating prototype scope. Fix it with **ObjectProvider**, **@Lookup** method injection, or a scoped proxy.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how Spring resolves dependencies at container startup and the lifecycle interaction between bean scopes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming Spring creates a new prototype instance each time the singleton uses it, when injection happens only once at singleton creation

sections.title: The Prototype-in-Singleton Injection Problem
sections.content:
Spring's **dependency injection** happens at bean creation time, not at method invocation time. When you inject a **prototype bean** into a **singleton bean**, Spring resolves that dependency once — when it creates the singleton during application startup. The singleton stores a reference to that single prototype instance and reuses it forever.

Think of it like a vending machine (singleton) that's supposed to dispense a fresh cup (prototype) each time, but it was built with one permanent cup attached. Every customer gets the same cup. The prototype loses its per-use semantics and effectively becomes a singleton.

This is a problem when the prototype holds **stateful data** like user-specific or per-request context. If UserSession is prototype-scoped but injected into a singleton OrderService, all users would share the same UserSession instance — a serious bug. The root cause is Spring's **eager dependency resolution**: it wires all dependencies when the container starts, not when your code calls a method. (And remember, singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM.)

sections.content:

sections.title: Prototype @Autowired into a singleton
Fetch a fresh prototype via ObjectProvider
Prototype Bean and the @Lookup Alternative
When This Problem Occurs
sections.content:
This issue appears when you mix **stateful prototype beans** with **singleton services**. Common scenarios: (1) a prototype holding per-request user context injected into a singleton REST controller — every request sees the same context. (2) a prototype with per-operation metrics injected into a singleton service — metrics from different operations get mixed. (3) a prototype builder with mutable state cached in a singleton — concurrent threads corrupt each other's state.

The problem doesn't occur if the prototype is truly stateless — but then you should just use singleton scope. Use ObjectProvider, @Lookup method injection, or scoped proxies whenever you need fresh prototype instances from a singleton.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting magic prototype behavior**: Learners assume marking a bean prototype makes Spring create new instances whenever it's used, even after injection. Spring only honors prototype at injection time — inject once into a singleton and you get one instance forever.
- **Using ApplicationContext.getBean() everywhere**: Some Learners scatter context.getBean(PrototypeBean.class) through their code, turning Spring into a service-locator anti-pattern. Use ObjectProvider — it's type-safe and built for this.
- **Marking beans prototype without justification**: If your bean has no mutable state, singleton is better. Prototype is only for beans that hold per-use state that can't be shared.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Injection time**: Spring resolves dependencies when creating the singleton, not when methods are called — the prototype is instantiated once
**Scope mismatch**: a longer-lived scope holding a shorter-lived one promotes the shorter scope to the longer scope's lifetime
**ObjectProvider<T>**: the recommended fix — call getObject() each time you need a fresh prototype
**@Lookup method injection**: annotate an abstract method returning the prototype; Spring returns a new instance per call
**Scoped proxy**: use @Scope(value="prototype", proxyMode=ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS) to inject a delegating proxy

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: The problem is that Spring injects dependencies when it creates the singleton bean, not when you call methods on it. So if you inject a prototype bean into a singleton using constructor or field injection, Spring creates that prototype instance once during application startup. The singleton holds onto that single instance forever, effectively making the prototype behave like a singleton. Let's say you have a RequestProcessor that's prototype-scoped because it holds request-specific data like a request ID. If you inject it directly into a singleton OrderService, every order processed by that service uses the same RequestProcessor with the same request ID. That defeats the whole purpose. The cleanest fix is ObjectProvider. Instead of injecting RequestProcessor directly, you inject ObjectProvider of RequestProcessor, then in your method you call provider dot getObject to get a fresh instance each time. Spring also supports @Lookup method injection where you define an abstract method that returns the prototype, and Spring implements it to return new instances. You can also use scoped proxies by setting proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS in the @Scope annotation, which makes Spring inject a proxy that delegates to fresh instances. The key thing to remember is that prototype scope only works at injection time — once injected, it's just a regular object reference.

beats.text: The prototype-in-singleton problem happens when you wire a prototype bean straight into a singleton. Spring injects it once at startup, and the singleton holds that one instance for life. And singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM.
Spring wires dependencies once, at startup. The singleton asks for a processor, Spring injects one prototype, and that's it. Nothing re-injects the field on later calls unless you design for it.

items: Wrong pattern: @Autowired processor in a singleton gives one instance for life.
ObjectProvider fix: inject ObjectProvider and call getObject for a fresh one.
@Lookup fix: Spring overrides an abstract method to return a new prototype each call.
getBean fix works but it's the service locator anti-pattern, so avoid it.

beats.text: Say TaskService is a @Service singleton and TaskProcessor is @Scope prototype with per-task state. Wire the processor in directly and every task shares it, so state from one bleeds into the next. Here's the non-obvious part. Injecting an ObjectProvider and calling getObject gives each task its own fresh processor.

items: The bug is silent. Spring never warns that the prototype degraded to singleton behavior.
Don't reach for getBean in your service layer. It's the service locator anti-pattern and hurts testing.

speakable_v2.cap: Wiring a prototype straight into a singleton silently breaks it. Use ObjectProvider or @Lookup for a fresh instance.
